The arc-eye hawkfish (Paracirrhites arcatus) exhibits life-history traits typical of a small-bodied coral reef predator. At a constant water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the embryonic development period is brief, with eggs hatching after just 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days]. This rapid eclosion is characteristic of many tropical teleosts, producing a yolk-sac larva that relies on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth for a newly emerged prolarva is extremely low, estimated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a consequence of the small egg diameter of approximately 0.8 mm. These lecithotrophic larvae drift as part of the ichthyoplankton for several weeks, during which they undergo flexion and the development of fin rays before transitioning to a benthic existence. Upon settling onto the reef, the young-of-year face intense predation pressure, which selects for rapid early growth rates to quickly exceed the gape limits of common invertebrate predators.

As juveniles grow, they begin to accumulate somatic tissue, and a key ontogenetic milestone is the attainment of puberty. The standard length at which this species reaches sexual maturity is 7.3 cm [Lp = 7.3 cm], a value derived from dissections of specimens from the central Indo-Pacific. Corresponding to this body size, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 4.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 4.2 grams], though this mass can vary modestly with local food availability and reef habitat quality. This weight marks the transition from a non-reproductive juvenile to a mature individual capable of vitellogenesis and spermiation. Males in this species tend to mature at a slightly smaller size than females, a pattern consistent with other protogynous or size-dimorphic members of the family Cirrhitidae. Field data indicate a mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 6% [GSI = 6%] for reproductively active adults sampled during the peak spawning season under ambient thermal regimes averaging 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C].

The ultimate standard length, representing the asymptotic body size that adults approach over their lifespan, has been estimated at 20 cm [Li = 20 cm] for the arc-eye hawkfish, a value consistent with the maximum sizes recorded in museum collections and underwater visual surveys. From this length, the corresponding ultimate wet weight can be derived using the length-weight relationship established for the species, yielding an estimate of 92 grams [Wwi = 92 grams] for a fully grown adult. This body mass places Paracirrhites arcatus among the medium-sized members of its genus, with individuals capable of attaining this mass only after several years of steady growth on the reef. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical cubic form, with females often reaching slightly heavier masses for a given length during the spawning season due to ovarian development. Territorial males, which defend prominent coral heads, tend to be among the heaviest individuals in a population, likely due to both their age and the energetic advantages of holding a high-quality feeding territory.

Regarding reproductive output, arc-eye hawkfish are iteroparous spawners that release pelagic eggs in multiple events over an extended breeding season. Each spawning event yields a modest number of eggs, and the daily reproductive rate for a mature female is reflected in the combination of spawning frequency and batch fecundity. Field observations indicate that females produce approximately 1 batch of eggs every 2 days during the peak summer months when water temperatures are elevated. The number of eggs released per batch has been quantified at roughly 200 to 300 eggs, a value that scales positively with female body size, with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to the annual reproductive output. These eggs are fertilized externally in the water column following a brief courtship ascent by the pair, after which the transparent, buoyant eggs drift away on ocean currents. The combination of frequent spawning and moderate batch fecundity results in a high lifetime fecundity, compensating for the elevated mortality rates experienced during the vulnerable pelagic larval phase.

The total lifespan of the arc-eye hawkfish has been estimated from otolith-based age validation studies, which indicate that individuals can survive for approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under natural reef conditions at a stable temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. This longevity is relatively high for a fish of its body size and is comparable to that of other long-lived coral reef predators such as groupers and snappers. Such an extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, with older individuals contributing a disproportionate share of the population's offspring due to their elevated fecundity and spawning frequency. Mortality in later years is largely attributed to predation by larger piscivores, including moray eels and sharks, as well as to senescence-related declines in physiological performance. The combination of a small birth mass, a long developmental period to maturity, and a lengthy adult lifespan places the arc-eye hawkfish along a slow end of the life-history continuum relative to many other small-bodied reef fishes, a strategy that appears well-suited to the relatively stable but competitive environment of the Indo-Pacific coral reefs it inhabits.
